## 📦 Version Updates

The latest stable release is 2.4.21, published on October 8, 2026, matching official release notes.

Kotlin 2.4.21 is an emergency quality hotfix addressing several critical defects exposed across multiplatform compiler backends and runtimes in the 2.4.20 GA release. For an overview of foundational enhancements introduced in the 2.4 series across the standard library, Native, and WebAssembly targets, check out our Kotlin 2.4 New Features Deep Dive.
Source: Kotlin Weekly #2: 2.4.21 Emergency Hotfix Arrives, KMP Drops Swift IDE Support, and Campfire JVM Throughput Rivals Rust — Dango Daily (https://daily.steinslab.io/en/lang/2026-10-12-kotlin-weekly-2026-w42/)

JetBrains: Kotlin 2.4.21 (Oct 8, 2026)

# Kotlin 2.4.21

Update· Oct 8, 2026· Not yet verified

Changelog Backend. Wasm - KT-89267 K/Wasm: calling a (T) -> R lambda with an argument that isn't a T traps instead of throwing ClassCastException JVM. Reflection - KT-89280 NoSuchElementException in argumentsMakeSenseOnlyForMutableContainer for Java non-static inner class of generic outer class - KT-80710 Reflection: change KCallable representation to avoid...
Source: JetBrains: Kotlin 2.4.21 (Oct 8, 2026) (https://releases.fru.dev/releases/kotlin-2026-10-08-kotlin-2-4-21)

## What I was able to confirm:

Kotlin 2.4.20 introduced coroutine stack trace recovery into the standard library, added new collection helper functions, and provided new kotlin.test overloads. This was a major release.

2.4.21 is the subsequent patch release. A Release Candidate for 2.4.21 was available via Gradle tooling as early as October 6th. Now, Dependabot PRs are being generated to bump Kotlin from 2.4.20 to 2.4.21 in Android projects.
Source: Kotlin 2.4.21 vs 2.4.20: The Patch Bump I Almost Ignored (https://medium.com/@androidlab/kotlin-2-4-21-vs-2-4-20-the-patch-bump-i-almost-ignored-d8618ec4ac39)

This comparison uses only what shipped and was documented by early November 2026. That means Kotlin 2.4.21 (October 8), Flutter 3.47 with its 3.47.8 security patch, and React Native 0.88 (October 19). We also flag three releases that are scheduled but not out: Kotlin 2.5.0, Flutter 3.50 and React Native 0.89. Where the public record has no neutral three-way benchmark, we say so and give you a protocol to run your own.

...

| Attribute | Kotlin Multiplatform | Flutter | React Native |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steward | JetBrains | Google | Meta (released 2015) |
| Language | Kotlin | Dart | JavaScript / TypeScript |
| Current stable | Kotlin 2.4.21 (Oct 8, 2026) | Flutter 3.47 (Aug 12, 2026), patched to 3.47.8 | React Native 0.88 (Oct 19, 2026) |
| Shared UI toolkit | Compose Multiplatform 1.12.2 (optional) | Flutter widgets (core) | React components mapped to native views |
| Status of the core tech | KMP stable since Nov 2023 | Mature, four stable releases planned for 2026 | Mature, a release roughly every two months |
| Android | Yes, first-class | Yes | Yes |
| iOS | Compose UI, or native SwiftUI/UIKit on top of shared logic | Yes, Xcode 27 prep done in 3.47 | Yes, SceneDelegate support added in 0.88 |
| Desktop | Compose Multiplatform lists macOS, Windows, Linux | macOS, Windows, Linux with Impeller by default since 3.47 | Not part of the core 0.88 announcement |
| Web | WebAssembly-capable browsers listed | Web target exists, Flutter 3.50 changes pending | Web-standard event dispatching now default |
| Rendering model | Native UI, or Compose’s own UI layer | Impeller renderer draws the UI | Native views via the New Architecture |
| Native interop | Direct, same-language access to platform APIs | Platform channels and plugins | TurboModules and Fabric components |
| Preview and reload tooling | Compose Hot Reload from the command line (Toolchain 0.12) | Widget Previews, stable in 3.47 | Metro 0.87 bundler |
| Release cadence | Language release, then a tooling release (2.x.20), then bug fixes | Feb, May, Aug, Nov stable windows | About six minor releases a year |
| Official license price | None listed in current official sources | None listed | None listed, open source |
| Next scheduled release | Kotlin 2.5.0, planned for December 2026 | Flutter 3.50, targeted for November 2026 | 0.89, not yet released |

...

## Current versions and what changed in the last three months

All three projects moved between August and early November 2026. The table lists the release that a new project should pin today, with its date and the headline change.

| Stack | Release to pin today | Date | Headline change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kotlin | 2.4.21 (bug-fix) | Oct 8, 2026 | Follows the 2.4.20 tooling release of Sep 7, 2026 |
| Compose Multiplatform | 1.12.2 stable | Oct 2026 | 1.13.0-beta01 previews iOS autofill and WebGL interop |
| Flutter | 3.47.8 | Nov 4, 2026 advisory | 3.47 brought Impeller to desktop by default (Aug 12) |
| React Native | 0.88 | Oct 19, 2026 | Web-standard events by default, variable fonts, React 19.3.0 |

Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta2 is out as a prerelease, and the official Kotlin release page plans 2.5.0 for December 2026 and 2.5.20 for March 2027. Treat the beta as a preview. It reportedly adds a Node.js provisioning toolchain, an npm-dependency DSL and a new Swift export DSL, which would replace the legacy swiftExport block with export.swift. Those details come from a single source and could change before the final build.

...

### What is the latest version of each framework?

As of November 4, 2026: Kotlin 2.4.21 with Compose Multiplatform 1.12.2, Flutter 3.47 (security patch 3.47.8), and React Native 0.88. Kotlin 2.5.0, Flutter 3.50 and React Native 0.89 are scheduled but were not confirmed as released.
Source: KMP vs Flutter vs React Native: 3 Tested, 1 Wins [2026] (https://tech-insider.org/kotlin-multiplatform-vs-flutter-vs-react-native-2026/)

questions.question: What does your side project mainly do with its data?

options.label: Relational, structured records
options.description: Users, orders, posts, etc. with clear relationships and you want joins + constraints enforced.

options.label: Mostly documents / JSON blobs
options.description: Nested, evolving, schema-less objects fetched whole (content, profiles, event payloads).

options.label: Key-value / cache / sessions
options.description: Simple lookups by key, counters, TTLs — speed matters more than querying.

options.label: Time-series, search, or graph-shaped
options.description: Metrics/events over time, full-text search, or heavily interconnected entities.

questions.question: How do you want to run it?

options.label: Managed cloud DB (Recommended)
options.description: Someone else handles backups/failover; you pay a monthly fee (Neon, Supabase, Atlas, RDS).

options.label: Free tier / zero cost to start
options.description: Hobby-tier limits are fine; you'll live with cold starts and small quotas.

options.label: Self-hosted in Docker/VPS
options.description: You want full control and no vendor lock-in; you'll own ops and backups.

options.label: Embedded / local-only
options.description: Runs inside the app process or a file on disk (SQLite, DuckDB) — no server at all.

questions.question: What's your expected scale and access pattern?

options.label: Tiny — a few users, read-heavy
options.description: Single small dataset, mostly reads, occasional writes.

options.label: Small but write-heavy
options.description: Logging, events, or chat-like writes; needs to handle bursts.

options.label: Growing — expect horizontal scale later
options.description: You want room to grow to many users/regions without a rewrite.

options.label: Globally distributed / offline-first
options.description: Users in many regions, or mobile clients that sync and work offline.

questions.question: What matters most in the trade-off?

options.label: Familiarity and speed of development
options.description: You want whatever you already know so you can ship fast.

options.label: Strong consistency and correctness
options.description: Transactions, constraints, and no data loss are non-negotiable.

options.label: Flexibility to change schema later
options.description: You're still discovering the data model and don't want migrations to hurt.

options.label: Lowest cost / no lock-in
options.description: Open standards, easy export, cheap at small scale.

title: [Data shape] What does your side project mainly do with its data?
options: 1. Relational, structured records — Users, orders, posts, etc. with clear relationships and you want joins + constraints enforced.
2. Mostly documents / JSON blobs — Nested, evolving, schema-less objects fetched whole (content, profiles, event payloads).
3. Key-value / cache / sessions — Simple lookups by key, counters, TTLs — speed matters more than querying.
4. Time-series, search, or graph-shaped — Metrics/events over time, full-text search, or heavily interconnected entities.

title: [Hosting] How do you want to run it?
options: 1. Managed cloud DB (Recommended) — Someone else handles backups/failover; you pay a monthly fee (Neon, Supabase, Atlas, RDS).
2. Free tier / zero cost to start — Hobby-tier limits are fine; you'll live with cold starts and small quotas.
3. Self-hosted in Docker/VPS — You want full control and no vendor lock-in; you'll own ops and backups.
4. Embedded / local-only — Runs inside the app process or a file on disk (SQLite, DuckDB) — no server at all.

title: [Scale] What's your expected scale and access pattern?
options: 1. Tiny — a few users, read-heavy — Single small dataset, mostly reads, occasional writes.
2. Small but write-heavy — Logging, events, or chat-like writes; needs to handle bursts.
3. Growing — expect horizontal scale later — You want room to grow to many users/regions without a rewrite.
4. Globally distributed / offline-first — Users in many regions, or mobile clients that sync and work offline.

title:
[Priority] What matters most in the trade-off?

1. Familiarity and speed of development — You want whatever you already know so you can ship fast.
2. Strong consistency and correctness — Transactions, constraints, and no data loss are non-negotiable.
3. Flexibility to change schema later — You're still discovering the data model and don't want migrations to hurt.
4. Lowest cost / no lock-in — Open standards, easy export, cheap at small scale.
